cards.back: To gradually gather or collect an increasing amount of something over time. "The company accumulated significant debt during the economic downturn." Common collocations: accumulate wealth, accumulate evidence, accumulate experience.

To accept or recognize the truth or existence of something. "The government acknowledged the need for urgent reforms in the education sector." Common collocations: acknowledge a problem, widely acknowledged, acknowledge the fact.

To change or adjust in order to suit new conditions or a different environment. "Students must adapt to new teaching methods when they enter university." Common collocations: adapt to change, adapt quickly, adapt a strategy.

Next to or very close to something, sharing a boundary or border. "The new library was built adjacent to the main university campus." Common collocations: adjacent to, adjacent area, adjacent building.

To publicly support or recommend a particular cause, policy, or action. "Many health professionals advocate a balanced diet and regular exercise." Common collocations: strongly advocate, advocate for change, advocate a policy.

Although; even though — used to introduce a concessive clause. "The project was completed on time, albeit at a higher cost than originally planned." Common collocations: albeit briefly, albeit slowly, albeit with difficulty.

Having more than one possible meaning or interpretation; unclear. "The wording of the contract was ambiguous, leading to a legal dispute." Common collocations: ambiguous statement, deliberately ambiguous, morally ambiguous.

To make changes to a document, law, or statement in order to improve or correct it. "Parliament voted to amend the existing legislation on data protection." Common collocations: amend the law, amend a constitution, amend a proposal.

A comparison between two things to highlight their similarities and explain a concept. "The professor drew an analogy between the human brain and a computer network." Common collocations: draw an analogy, by analogy, close analogy.

To understand the full significance of something or to recognize its value. "It is important to appreciate the complexity of climate change before proposing solutions." Common collocations: fully appreciate, appreciate the importance, greatly appreciate.

Based on random choice or personal whim rather than any reason or system. "The selection criteria appeared arbitrary and lacked any transparent methodology." Common collocations: arbitrary decision, arbitrary rule, seem arbitrary.

The right or condition of self-governance; independence in decision-making. "The university grants its departments a high degree of autonomy in curriculum design." Common collocations: personal autonomy, grant autonomy, degree of autonomy.

An inclination or prejudice for or against a person, group, or idea, often considered unfair. "The study was criticized for potential bias in the way participants were selected." Common collocations: cultural bias, confirmation bias, bias towards.

Able to exist or work together without conflict or contradiction. "The new software must be compatible with the existing operating systems." Common collocations: compatible with, fully compatible, mutually compatible.

To add to something in a way that enhances or improves it; to make complete. "Practical training sessions complement the theoretical knowledge gained in lectures." Common collocations: complement each other, perfect complement, complement a strategy.

To act in accordance with a rule, demand, or request. "All manufacturers must comply with the new environmental regulations by the end of the year." Common collocations: comply with regulations, fail to comply, comply fully.

To form an idea or plan in the mind; to imagine or think of something. "It is difficult to conceive of a world without access to digital technology." Common collocations: conceive an idea, originally conceived, difficult to conceive.

To keep or restrict someone or something within certain limits or boundaries. "The discussion should be confined to the main topic of the meeting." Common collocations: confine to, confined space, confine oneself to.

To comply with rules, standards, or social expectations; to behave according to accepted norms. "Students are expected to conform to the code of conduct outlined in the handbook." Common collocations: conform to standards, conform to expectations, pressure to conform.

A general agreement among a group of people on a particular matter. "After lengthy deliberation, the committee reached a consensus on the proposed budget." Common collocations: reach a consensus, general consensus, build consensus.

To be a part of a whole; to form or make up something. "Women constitute approximately half of the total workforce in the country." Common collocations: constitute a threat, constitute a majority, constitute a violation.

To think about something carefully and at length; to consider as a possibility. "The government is contemplating new measures to reduce carbon emissions." Common collocations: contemplate a change, contemplate the future, seriously contemplate.

To assert the opposite of a statement or to be inconsistent with something. "The new findings contradict the results of earlier research on the same topic." Common collocations: directly contradict, contradict each other, contradict a theory.

Standards or principles by which something is judged or decided (plural of criterion). "Applicants must meet several criteria to be eligible for the scholarship programme." Common collocations: meet the criteria, selection criteria, strict criteria.

To be a sign of something; to indicate or represent a particular meaning. "In this diagram, the red arrows denote the direction of blood flow through the heart." Common collocations: denote a change, commonly denote, denote the presence of.

To show or represent something in a picture, story, or description. "The documentary depicts the daily struggles of families living below the poverty line." Common collocations: accurately depict, depict a scene, vividly depict.
To obtain or receive something from a specified source. "Many English words derive from Latin and Greek roots." Common collocations: derive from, derive benefit, derive pleasure.

To depart from an established course, standard, or norm. "The results deviate significantly from what was originally predicted by the model." Common collocations: deviate from the norm, deviate from a plan, deviate significantly.

Showing a great deal of variety; including people from many different backgrounds. "The city has a diverse population with residents from over 150 different countries." Common collocations: culturally diverse, diverse range, diverse community.

Characterized by constant change, activity, or progress; energetic and forceful. "The technology sector is one of the most dynamic areas of the global economy." Common collocations: dynamic environment, dynamic process, highly dynamic.

To gradually wear away or diminish something over time. "Public trust in the institution has been eroded by a series of corruption scandals." Common collocations: erode confidence, erode trust, gradually erode.

To assess or judge the value, quality, or importance of something carefully. "Teachers evaluate student performance through a combination of exams and coursework." Common collocations: evaluate performance, critically evaluate, evaluate the effectiveness.

To go beyond a set limit, expectation, or standard; to be greater than. "The company's annual revenue exceeded ten million dollars for the first time." Common collocations: exceed expectations, exceed a limit, far exceed.

To make full use of a resource or opportunity, sometimes unfairly for personal gain. "Some companies exploit cheap labour in developing countries to maximize profits." Common collocations: exploit resources, exploit a weakness, exploit an opportunity.

Possible and practical to accomplish; capable of being done or carried out. "The engineers concluded that building a tunnel beneath the river was technically feasible." Common collocations: economically feasible, feasible solution, technically feasible.

Having limits or bounds; not infinite in quantity or extent. "The Earth's natural resources are finite and must be managed sustainably." Common collocations: finite resources, finite number, finite amount.

To encourage the development or growth of something; to promote or nurture. "The programme aims to foster creativity and critical thinking among young learners." Common collocations: foster growth, foster innovation, foster a sense of.

A proposed explanation made on the basis of limited evidence as a starting point for investigation. "The researchers tested the hypothesis that sleep deprivation affects memory retention." Common collocations: test a hypothesis, support a hypothesis, formulate a hypothesis.

To force something to be accepted, endured, or put in place by authority. "The government decided to impose stricter regulations on the financial industry." Common collocations: impose sanctions, impose restrictions, impose a ban.

Something that motivates or encourages a person to take a particular action. "Tax reductions serve as an incentive for companies to invest in renewable energy." Common collocations: financial incentive, provide an incentive, strong incentive.

To include something as part of a whole; to take in or contain as part of a system. "The new curriculum incorporates elements of both traditional and modern teaching methods." Common collocations: incorporate into, fully incorporate, incorporate feedback.

The basic physical and organizational structures needed for the operation of a society. "Significant investment in infrastructure is required to improve the transportation network." Common collocations: transport infrastructure, infrastructure development, basic infrastructure.

The quality of being honest and having strong moral principles; the state of being whole. "Academic integrity requires that students submit only their own original work." Common collocations: academic integrity, personal integrity, structural integrity.

To come between parties in a dispute or to take action to alter the course of events. "The central bank may intervene in the currency market to stabilize exchange rates." Common collocations: intervene in, government intervene, intervene early.

Conforming to the law or to accepted rules and standards; valid and justifiable. "Citizens have a legitimate right to question the decisions made by their government." Common collocations: legitimate concern, legitimate reason, perfectly legitimate.

To reduce something to the smallest possible amount, degree, or extent. "Safety procedures are designed to minimize the risk of accidents in the workplace." Common collocations: minimize risk, minimize costs, minimize the impact.

To discuss something in order to reach an agreement; to find a way over or through an obstacle. "The union plans to negotiate better working conditions for its members." Common collocations: negotiate a deal, negotiate terms, negotiate with.

Something that is usual, typical, or standard; an accepted standard of behaviour. "Working from home has become the norm for many employees since the pandemic." Common collocations: social norm, cultural norm, become the norm.

The official procedure or system of rules governing affairs of state or diplomatic occasions. "All staff must follow the safety protocol during an emergency evacuation." Common collocations: follow protocol, safety protocol, strict protocol.

Relating to or affecting the fundamental nature of something; far-reaching or thorough. "The company underwent radical changes in its management structure." Common collocations: radical change, radical reform, radical approach.
